content.text: With SSR, Angular can hand the server's
responses to the browser so it doesn't fetch them again, but only for eligible requests: by default

, without auth headers or credentials, with no cache directives that forbid it, requested the same way in the browser, during the initial render. Everything else is fetched twice, often because of one interceptor.

A store's product page is server-rendered, and its HTML already contains the name, the price and the reviews. Yet right after load, the Network panel shows the browser requesting the product, the reviews and the related items again, and the API now sees every page view twice. The team expected the transfer cache to prevent exactly this. The cause is the auth interceptor: it attaches an
header to every request, the public catalog included, and requests carrying that header are left out of the transfer cache by default.
The belief: the server already fetched everything the page needed, and SSR hands all of it to the browser, so a server-rendered app never calls the API twice for the same data.
The belief comes from a real feature that's on by default.
response caching on the server and transfers that cache to the client "to avoid extra HTTP requests", in the words of its API docs. In a starter app, where every request is an anonymous
, the Network panel confirms it: no duplicates. Real apps add interceptors,

A one-time handoff, not an HTTP cache

, and responses that set a cookie. In Angular 22's implementation, that check sees the request as it leaves your interceptors, so a header an interceptor adds counts exactly as if you had written it yourself.

That's the opening story. The exclusions exist so that one user's responses don't end up serialized into a page, and an interceptor that authenticates everything makes every request look user-specific.

content.text: The fix doesn't touch the cache settings. Public data goes out without credentials, so it qualifies on its own, and requests that really are personal keep their header and are fetched again in the browser, which is the safe outcome.
The browser has to ask the same question

A stored response is found by the request's details: in Angular 22's implementation, the method, the URL, the query parameters, the body and the response type. If the browser's request differs, it's a miss. Two common causes:

blocks.title: Find the duplicates in one reload

content.text: Open the Network panel, filter on Fetch/XHR and reload a server-rendered page. Every API request that fires before you touch anything is a request the server probably made already. Check each one against the table above.

blocks.title: Opting in can leak one user's data

content.text: all serialize responses into the HTML. If that HTML is stored by a
such as a CDN, the next visitor can receive the previous user's data, including fields the page never displayed. Enable them only for responses that are the same for everyone.
How to apply it in your project
Reload a few key server-rendered pages with the Network panel open, and list the API calls the browser repeats.
